det_01.label: Origin: The Economist's 'TV's golden age is real' (24 Nov 2018)
det_01.content: This dataset was assembled by The Economist's Graphic Detail team for an article titled 'TV's golden age is real,' published on 24 November 2018. The piece used IMDb user ratings for every American TV drama series available on IMDb from 1990 to 2018 to ask whether the cultural intuition about a 'Golden Age of TV' is supported by audience scoring. The published chart was a scatter of season-by-season average IMDb ratings against premiere date, with the premise that if quality has truly risen since the late 1990s the dot cloud should drift upward over time. The CSV provided is exactly the data that drove that scatter plot. Each row is one season of one drama, with seven fields: titleId (IMDb tt-id), seasonNumber, title, the season's premiere date, av_rating (the season's average rating on IMDb), share (what fraction of total votes that season received), and a comma-separated genre tag. The data file ships with a README that names IMDb, OMDb (for region/airing dates), and The Economist's own scripting as the three sources.

det_02.label: What 'Golden Age' means in TV criticism (1999 → ~2023)
det_02.content: When critics talk about a contemporary 'Golden Age' of television they mean a roughly 25-year stretch beginning with HBO's The Sopranos in January 1999 and running through the prestige-drama explosion of the 2000s and 2010s. Wikipedia's reference article dates the period 2000–2023; The Sopranos is the canonical opening shot. The era is defined by cinematic production budgets, serialized rather than episodic storytelling, and morally ambiguous anti-hero leads — Tony Soprano, Don Draper, Walter White, Stringer Bell. Production values on shows like Mad Men, Breaking Bad, and Band of Brothers came to rival theatrical film, and HBO's blueprint was copied first by AMC (Mad Men 2007, Breaking Bad 2008) and then aggressively by Netflix (House of Cards 2013) and the rest of the streamers. Crucially for this dataset, almost the entire 'Golden Age' falls inside the 1990–2018 window the IMDb data covers — so if it really happened, it should be visible in the ratings.

det_03.label: Peak TV: explosion of scripted series 2002 → 2018
det_03.content: Parallel to the rise in quality is a separate but related story: the sheer *number* of original scripted series exploded. FX boss John Landgraf, who has tracked the count for two decades, recorded 182 scripted series in 2002, 343 by 2013, 487 by 2017, then 559 in 2021 and a peak of 600 in 2022. Within the dataset window (through 2018), the count roughly tripled. Landgraf's coinage 'Peak TV' captured the worry that quality could not keep pace with quantity — by 2018 he was already calling it a 'Gilded Age' rather than a Golden one. This matters for the data because the scatter must be denser at the right (more shows = more dots) without being meaningfully *higher* if Landgraf was right. If the dot cloud rises *and* gets denser, both the Golden Age and the Peak TV theses are supported.

det_04.label: IMDb rating bias: self-selection, fan-survivorship, recency
det_04.content: Before treating IMDb scores as 'TV quality' it is worth knowing how those scores are made. IMDb ratings are aggregated 1–10 votes from a self-selected pool of registered users, which produces three structural biases: (1) self-selection — viewers who feel strongly are over-represented and middling opinions disappear; (2) fan survivorship — people who watch a season to the end and then rate it tend to be fans, which inflates television scores relative to films; (3) early-rating skew — the first wave of voters is the most enthusiastic, so brand-new seasons land higher and drift down later. Average drama ratings on IMDb cluster around 8 out of 10 — far above the theoretical midpoint of 5.5 — for exactly this reason. The infamous Game of Thrones final-season collapse (the series finale fell to 4.0/10, the lowest score in any of the show's eight seasons) is the same mechanism running in reverse: angry viewers self-select to vote down. None of this kills the dataset as a tool for spotting trends; it just means absolute levels say more about who shows up to vote than about objective quality, while differences between seasons and shows are still meaningful.

det_05.label: Why this matters: TV is the dominant cultural form of the streaming era
det_05.content: Asking whether TV drama is genuinely getting better is not a niche aesthetic question. By 2018, when this dataset was assembled, the average American household watched several hours of scripted television daily, streaming services were displacing theatrical film as the cultural centerpiece, and HBO/Netflix originals were displacing Hollywood films at the Emmys and in critic year-end lists. If the perceived 'Golden Age' is real — if quality really has risen — that is a story about how an entire art form re-organized itself around the long-form serialized drama in less than two decades. If it is illusory — if we have just been telling ourselves a flattering story while watching a few hits and ignoring the floor — that matters too, because policymakers, advertisers, and an entire cultural-criticism industry have built their narratives on the assumption that the Golden Age is settled fact.

det_06.label: Interpretive hook: rising floor vs. rising ceiling
det_06.content: There is a subtle distinction worth holding on to before looking at the numbers. A 'Golden Age' could mean two very different things in the data: either the *ceiling* has risen (the very best shows in 2015 are better than the very best shows in 1995) or the *floor* has risen (mediocre 2015 dramas are better than mediocre 1995 dramas, while the top stays similar). Most cultural critics talk as though both are true. But IMDb's structural ceiling sits around 9.5 — Breaking Bad's final seasons, Band of Brothers, Chernobyl all bunch up there. So if there is room to move it is mainly the *floor* that can rise. Watch for that distinction: a clear upward drift in the *median* season rating is stronger evidence than an upward drift in the *maximum*, because the max is capped by IMDb's voting culture itself.

det_07.label: Scope suggestion for the analyst
det_07.content: Concrete things worth measuring: (1) median av_rating per premiere year, smoothed — this is the cleanest test of the Golden Age hypothesis; (2) top decile vs. bottom decile of av_rating per year — separates 'rising ceiling' from 'rising floor'; (3) count of seasons per year — visualises Peak TV; (4) which shows produce the biggest within-show jumps and drops (Game of Thrones falling off a cliff in season 8 is the prototype); (5) which genres rise fastest — does the Golden Age belong to drama-only, or also crime/sci-fi/fantasy? (6) the relationship between 'share' (votes) and av_rating — do the most-voted seasons rate higher, lower, or unrelated? Do not over-interpret absolute scores; absolute IMDb means cluster near 8 because of self-selection. Differences between years and within shows are far more informative than levels.
